words.gloss: the wealth of the ear (gained by listening)

ai.literal: Among wealth, the wealth is the wealth of the ear; that wealth, among all wealth, is supreme.
ai.translation: The wealth of the ear, gained by listening to the wise, is the greatest of all wealth; that wealth is supreme among every other kind of treasure.
ai.modern: செல்வங்களுள் சிறந்த செல்வம் காதால் கேட்டுப் பெறும் செல்வமே ஆகும்; அந்தச் செல்வம் மற்ற எல்லாச் செல்வங்களுள்ளும் முதன்மையானதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet introduces the chapter on listening (hearing) by elevating it above all material possessions. The compound 'செவிச்செல்வம்' (wealth of the ear) refers to the wisdom and knowledge acquired by listening to learned people. The poet repeats the word 'செல்வம்' (wealth) multiple times to emphasize that listening is not merely a sensory act but the most valuable asset a person can acquire. Among all forms of worldly riches, this intellectual wealth is declared to be 'தலை' (supreme or foremost) because it cannot be stolen and guides one's life safely.

ai.literal: When there is no food for the ear, a little should be offered even to the stomach.
ai.translation: When there is no food of wisdom for the ear to feast upon, only then should a little food be offered to the stomach.
ai.modern: காதுக்குக் கேட்கும் அறிவு உணவு இல்லாத பொழுது, வயிற்றுக்கும் சிறிதளவு உணவு கொடுக்கப்பட வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet beautifully contrasts intellectual nourishment with physical sustenance. The poet metaphorically describes listening to wise teachings as 'food for the ear'. Physical food for the stomach is treated as a secondary necessity, to be taken only in small measures when the mind is not actively engaged in learning. By prioritizing the hunger of the ears over the hunger of the stomach, the couplet elevates the pursuit of knowledge above mere physical existence.

ai.literal: Those who possess learning by listening, which is food for the ear, are equal to those who are perfected by sacrificial food, on this earth.
ai.translation: Those on earth who feast on learning through their ears are equal to the celestial beings who feed on sacrificial offerings.
ai.modern: செவிக்கு உணவாகிய கேள்வி ஞானத்தைப் பெற்றவர்கள், இவ்வுலகில் வாழ்ந்தாலும், வேள்வித் தீயின் அவியுணவை உண்ணும் தேவர்களுக்கு ஒப்பானவர்கள் ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet elevates the status of those who acquire wisdom by listening. The poet compares the physical food of the gods, which is the sacrificial offering (அவியுணவு), to the intellectual food of humans, which is listening to wise words (செவியுணவு). Those who feed their ears with knowledge while living on this earth (நிலத்து) are considered equal to the immortal celestial beings (ஆன்றார்) who are sustained by sacrifices. Through this comparison, the act of listening to wisdom is shown to be a divine sustenance that elevates mortal humans to a god-like state.

ai.literal: Even if one has not learned, let him listen; that, to a person, in times of weakness, will be a supporting staff.
ai.translation: Even if a person has not learned through formal study, let them listen to the wise; in times of weakness and distress, that acquired knowledge will serve as a steadying staff.
ai.modern: ஒருவர் நூல்களைக் கற்கவில்லை என்றாலும், கற்றறிந்தவர்களின் சொற்களைக் கேட்க வேண்டும்; அப்படிக் கேட்பது அவருக்குத் தளர்ச்சி வரும் காலத்தில் ஊன்றுகோல் போன்ற துணையாக இருக்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the immense value of listening as a source of wisdom, especially for those who lack formal education. Even if a person has not studied books, they should actively listen to the words of the wise. In times of mental or physical weakness and vulnerability, the wisdom gathered through listening acts like a sturdy staff that prevents them from falling. The metaphor of the supporting staff beautifully illustrates how oral learning provides stability and guidance during life's difficult moments.

words.gloss: a support staff or walking stick

ai.literal: Like a support staff in a place that has slipping, are the words from the mouth of those who possess good conduct.
ai.translation: The words from the mouth of those who possess disciplined conduct are like a supporting staff on slippery ground.
ai.modern: வழுக்கல் நிறைந்த இடத்தில் ஊன்றுகோல் உதவுவது போல, நல்ல ஒழுக்கம் உடையவர்களின் வாயிலிருந்து வரும் சொற்கள் வாழ்க்கையின் தடுமாற்றங்களில் துணையாக உதவும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the protective value of listening to virtuous people. Just as a walking staff prevents a person from slipping and falling on wet, unstable ground, the wise words spoken by those of disciplined conduct act as a reliable support during difficult times. Listening to their guidance saves one from moral and practical downfalls in life.

ai.literal: Even a tiny bit good things let one listen to, to that same extent abundant greatness it will yield.
ai.translation: Let a person listen to good things, however small they may be; even to that small extent, it will yield abundant greatness.
ai.modern: எவ்வளவு சிறிதளவாக இருந்தாலும் நல்ல விஷயங்களைக் கேட்க வேண்டும்; அந்தக் கேட்ட அளவிற்கு அது நிறைந்த பெருமையைத் தரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the immense value of listening to wise and virtuous words, regardless of how brief or small the instruction might be. The poet uses the correlative terms 'எனைத்தானும்' (however small) and 'அனைத்தானும்' (to that very extent) to show a direct proportion between listening and gaining dignity. Even a tiny drop of good advice, when heard and absorbed, translates into a corresponding measure of deep, abundant greatness for the listener. Therefore, one should never dismiss good words as insignificant, for every bit of listening contributes to one's character.

ai.literal: Even if they mistakenly understand, foolishness will not speak they who have subtly analyzed and accumulated learning by listening.
ai.translation: Those who have acquired deep knowledge by listening and subtly analyzing things will never utter foolish words, even if they happen to misunderstand something.

ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the profound impact of 'கேள்வி' (learning by listening to the wise). Those who have carefully analyzed and accumulated such knowledge possess a refined mind. Even if they occasionally misunderstand a concept ('பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும்'), their deep-rooted wisdom prevents them from speaking foolishly ('பேதைமை சொல்லார்'). The key words 'இழைத்துணர்ந்து' (subtly analyzing) and 'ஈண்டிய' (accumulated) emphasize that true listening is an active, deep process that safeguards one's speech from ignorance.

ai.literal: Even if hearing, not hearing nature indeed are, by listening, to be pierced not undergone, ears.
ai.translation: Ears that have not been pierced by listening to wise instructions, even if they can hear, are indeed of the nature of the deaf.
ai.modern: கேள்வி அறிவினால் துளைக்கப்படாத காதுகள், கேட்கும் தன்மை உடையனவாக இருந்தாலும், கேட்காத செவிடான தன்மையையே உடையனவாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme value of learning through listening. The poet uses a powerful metaphor, comparing ears that have not been 'pierced' or opened by listening to wise teachings to those of a deaf person. Even if these ears can physically hear sounds, they are functionally useless because they do not absorb meaningful knowledge. True hearing is not just the physical perception of sound, but the active reception of wisdom.

ai.literal: Those who are not of refined listening, to become of humble mouth is rare.
ai.translation: It is rare for those who have not acquired refined learning through listening to speak with humble and respectful words.
ai.modern: நுட்பமான கேள்வி அறிவு இல்லாதவர்கள், அடக்கமான சொற்களைப் பேசுபவர்களாக மாறுவது கடினம்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the direct connection between listening and the quality of one's speech. 'Nuṇaṅkiya' refers to subtle, sharp, and highly refined wisdom, while 'kēḷvi' is the act of listening to the wise. Those who do not cultivate this refined listening lack the inner maturity and restraint required for polite discourse. Consequently, it is extremely rare for such people to speak with a 'humble mouth' (vaṇaṅkiya vāy), which represents respectful and modest speech.

ai.literal: In the ear taste not-perceiving, mouth perception's beast-like people, even if they perish, even if they live, what does it matter?
ai.translation: What does it matter whether they live or die—those beast-like people who only know the taste of the mouth, but have never experienced the relish of the ear?
ai.modern: செவியால் கேட்கும் சுவையை உணராமல், வாயின் சுவையை மட்டுமே உணரும் விலங்கு போன்ற மனிதர்கள், இறந்தால் என்ன, வாழ்ந்தால் என்ன?
ai.explanation: This couplet concludes the chapter on listening by contrasting the refined pleasure of hearing wisdom with the basic physical pleasure of eating. The author uses the word 'taste' (சுவை) for both senses, comparing the 'taste of the ear' (listening to wise words) with the 'taste of the mouth' (eating food). Those who only seek physical nourishment and ignore intellectual growth are described as 'மாக்கள்' (beast-like people). The couplet bluntly asks what difference it makes to the world whether such unthinking people live or die, as their lives lack any meaningful purpose.
